# MMCATS Modern

MMCATS Modern replaces an obsolete Rails asset register with a separate implementation organized around identified legacy obligations: behavioral parity, domain constraints, authorization, auditability and reproducible local verification. The [engineering case study](https://mohd.paramasvara.online/en/mmcats-modern/) explains discovery → contracts → implementation → verification; the [parity matrix](docs/LEGACY_PARITY_MATRIX.md) connects the historical evidence to those contracts.

A server-rendered asset register implemented with **Rails 8.1.4, Ruby 4.0.7 and PostgreSQL 18.6**. Kubernetes/Helm is the primary deployment target; Docker/Podman Compose uses the same production OCI image.

Implemented: invite-only authentication, admin/editor/viewer permissions, company/division/staff CRUD, full asset attributes, search/sort/pagination, idempotent disposal/restoration and private Active Storage documents. Only synthetic development data is authorized. Production policy and real-data migration remain gated by [D-01–D-12](docs/DECISION_LOG.md). No license grant is provided.

Latest recorded [Render Free acceptance](docs/RENDER_FREE_ACCEPTANCE.md), **22 October 2026**: **66 tests / 568 assertions**, zero failures/errors/skips, a 38-check read-only viewer contract and local Docker/kind/Podman compatibility checks. Render/Neon/R2 provider acceptance and public application deployment remain unverified; strict emulated AMD64 load failed. Source publication does not grant security clearance or authorize deployment.

Earlier [21 October runtime exposure verification](docs/P0_RUNTIME_EXPOSURE_REPORT.md) recorded 61 tests / 518 assertions, encrypted isolated restores and passing measured native startup/resource budgets. Those measurements do not certify the later AMD64 artifact. The latest web scan still reports **43 HIGH / 1 UNKNOWN**; release remains blocked pending scoped security and operational decisions.

## Local demonstration

For the existing locally reviewed images, from this directory with Docker Desktop running (a fresh clone must first follow the [image build/provenance notes](deploy/postgres/README.md); the pinned images are local artifacts, not published registry downloads):

```sh
tools/init-local                 # first run only; preserves an existing .env
tools/compose-reviewed config --quiet
tools/compose-reviewed up -d --no-build
# New empty synthetic deployments only:
tools/compose-reviewed run --rm -e ALLOW_SYNTHETIC_SEED=1 migrate bin/rails db:seed
```

Open **http://127.0.0.1:13000**. The synthetic administrator email/password are in the ignored, permission-restricted `.env` generated by `tools/init-local`. Credentials are not printed or committed. Files and database records persist in scoped named volumes. Use `tools/compose-reviewed stop web db` to retain all data. Reviewed images are local artifacts; see [build/provenance](deploy/postgres/README.md) before rebuilding or transferring them. Never reuse an old Debian database volume with the reviewed Alpine image.

## Verification and operations

[Runbook](docs/RUNBOOK.md) contains Kubernetes, Compose, local development, backup/restore and smoke-test procedures. [Progress](docs/PROGRESS.md), [implementation report](docs/IMPLEMENTATION_REPORT.md), [security review](docs/SECURITY_REVIEW.md), [performance evidence](docs/PERFORMANCE_BASELINE.md) and [parity matrix](docs/LEGACY_PARITY_MATRIX.md) distinguish observed results from remaining gates. P0 is not complete until all required deployment/security gates have passed.

The [archived legacy repository](https://github.com/MohdVara/mmcats-legacy) is a static historical reference, not a code/runtime dependency. It and the private original remain unchanged. Public source publication was authorized by the owner on 22 October 2026 at [MohdVara/mmcats-modern](https://github.com/MohdVara/mmcats-modern). Historical reports retain their original no-publication state. This authorization covers source only; application deployment, provider accounts/billing and unresolved release gates remain separate. See the [publication and commit guide](docs/SOURCE_PUBLICATION.md).

# Legacy parity and requirement traceability

Legacy evidence is VERIFIED-STATIC, not runtime success. Targets below implement provisional synthetic-development policy (D-01–D-12). Status starts pending and is reconciled to observed tests at each milestone. Production policy and historical conversion remain gated.

## Coverage interpretation

26 BP cases are considered. 23 have implemented provisional local contracts with passing targeted tests. BP-14, BP-20 and BP-25 have passing local subsets but remain PARTIAL because historical state/date conversion and final financial policy are not approved or implemented. These are not 26 production-approved parity certifications. FR-16 required audit subset is implemented by finalization; general timeline and FR-17 remain deferred; FR-13 implements an explicit HTML-only exclusion. The test paths above are relative to `test/` where abbreviated. Original historical behavior remains unverified at runtime.

## Closeout regression (20 October 2026)

The 43-test/391-assertion suite passed on the reviewed PostgreSQL 18.6 image and after fixture credential hardening. Production-config role/asset/lifecycle/private-file checks passed on Compose and Kubernetes. Business app/config/migration behavior is preserved: 23 provisional BP contracts remain passing and BP-14/20/25 remain partial. Container fixes do not certify historical runtime or conversion. See [P0 closeout](P0_CLOSEOUT_REPORT.md).

43 tests remain, with permanent-deletion cases explicitly opting into the new policy;
new tests also prove default admin deletion denial. 23 complete provisional BP

unapproved detailed policies, not for absent MYR/MYT decisions.

# MMCATS — Legacy Asset Management System

Originally developed around 2015 as a college/diploma final project (owner-provided context), MMCATS is an asset register from an earlier stage of the owner's engineering development. It manages organizational assets, companies, divisions, staff, users and related attachments.

**Unmaintained historical software — not production-ready.** Known security and correctness limitations remain. No successful application boot, test-suite execution or business workflow has been verified in this assessment. Do not deploy it publicly or use it with real personal information.

## Original technology and architecture

The source establishes Ruby on Rails 4.1.8, Devise 3.4.1, SQLite configuration, ERB, the historical Rails asset pipeline and Bootstrap/jQuery-era frontend references. This archive does not independently verify a MySQL, Azure or Nginx deployment.

Six database entities form a Rails monolith: assets hold register/financial/lifecycle fields; companies and divisions represent organizations; staffs represent people referenced by assets; uploads store binary attachment content; users hold Devise authentication data. Source workflows cover CRUD, name search, sorting, five-row pagination, disposal/restore and attachment upload/download. These are static source observations, not successful runtime demonstrations.

Every included historical application file is byte-identical to the private original, including its original style and defects. Four previously substituted configuration/seed files are now **excluded entirely**: config/secrets.yml, config/initializers/devise.rb, config/environments/development.rb and db/seeds.rb. They contained original sensitive material or an identifier awaiting clearance; no modified versions or impersonating placeholders remain at those paths.

The inspectable snapshot is incomplete for safety/licensing reasons. Branding, unreviewed bundled third-party JS/CSS/fonts, generated assets, binaries and original Git history are also excluded. Missing essential initialization files and assets mean no boot/build/run claim is possible. The forensic documentation is newly authored evidence about the private original; its explicit publication adaptations do not change historical code or improve old findings.

# PACE-RAG

**PACE-RAG = Portfolio Assistant with Cited Evidence — Retrieval-Augmented Generation.**

- **P — Portfolio:** the professional evidence the assistant helps visitors explore.
- **A — Assistant:** an interface for finding reviewed information and relevant sources.
- **C — Cited:** direct answers retain validated supporting citations.
- **E — Evidence:** approved records bound what the system can substantiate.
- **RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation:** the architectural approach and direction, with retrieved evidence constraining any future generative path.

This is the official meaning going forward, not a claim about the project's historical naming origin. The current implementation primarily uses reviewed cached answers, deterministic technology composition and local retrieval. Live generative inference is currently disabled: the name does not mean that every query invokes a generative model. This evidence-first design favors traceable sources, reviewed reuse and conservative abstention.

Browser-first knowledge retrieval shared by the portfolio assistant and an inspectable Engineering RAG Lab with implementation documentation and synthetic examples. Search does not require Cloudflare credentials. Live generation is disabled by default.

Hosted demo: [PACE-RAG](https://pace-rag.paramasvara.online/), served by Cloudflare Pages. See [hosting](docs/HOSTING.md) for deployment and custom-domain setup. A hosted build may differ from local work; the [v1.6 activation review](docs/PACE-RAG-V1.6.1-RETRIEVAL-REVIEW.md) records the last checked local/hosted boundary.

PACE-RAG demonstrates how a small, curated knowledge base can answer questions with traceable sources, explicit provenance and conservative handling of unsupported claims. The current local implementation and workspace package are **v1.6.2 / `1.6.2`**. Historical foundation, UX and ontology reports retain their recorded versions; see the [current review](docs/PACE-RAG-V1.6.1-RETRIEVAL-REVIEW.md) for regression measurements and pending independent evaluation.

## What this repository contains

Start with the [portfolio case study](https://mohd.paramasvara.online/en/pace-rag-case-study/) for the source-bound answer example and architectural decisions. To inspect the implementation, follow [retrieval and provenance boundaries](docs/IMPLEMENTATION.md), [current recorded evaluation](docs/PACE-RAG-V1.6.1-RETRIEVAL-REVIEW.md) and the local commands below. Supported cached answers and technology composition are distinct from semantic suggestions and abstention; the optional generation gateway remains experimental and unverified in production.

- **Three searchable sources:** Professional Experience, How PACE-RAG Works, and Fictional Test Documents. Each has its own starters and browsable source library.
- **Local retrieval:** browser-based semantic search using a pinned embedding model, with keyword search available without the model.
- **Evidence-backed answers:** publication-approved cached answers, bounded technology summaries, source citations, and explicit abstention when a direct answer is unsupported.
- **Inspectable behavior:** ranking details, source snapshots, provenance, evaluation reports and six labelled failure simulations.
- **Technology understanding:** a curated registry of entities, aliases, categories and relationships, kept separate from owner-confirmed project usage.
- **Reusable integration:** a React assistant package and the native portfolio adapter near About.
- **Optional server scaffolding:** a Cloudflare Worker gateway with request verification and SQLite budget coordination. It is disabled in the standalone app and is not a production-verified service.

## How it works

```text
Content records + approvals + technology evidence
                       |
              Validate, chunk and index
                       |
          Hash-verified static knowledge assets
                       |
       Select one of three scoped source views
                       |
     Cached answer / technology composition / retrieval
                       |
       Cited answer, related sources or abstention
```

Indexing produces immutable knowledge releases and, when requested, embedding vectors. The browser verifies assets before deriving the selected source view. Exact cached answers and supported technology questions can avoid model initialization; other semantic queries load the model on demand. Opening retrieval details displays the existing result. Ordinary local search does not call a hosted LLM.

# Hotel Booking Constraint API

A **historical 2019 interview exercise** in Node.js/Express: allocate guests to rooms using a small rule parser, with controller tests for accepted and rejected bookings. This repository demonstrates an earlier approach to business-rule modeling; it has not been modernized or assessed as a production booking service.

[Current engineering portfolio](https://mohd.paramasvara.online/en/) · [Professional work and contact](https://mohd.paramasvara.online/en/work-with-me/)

## Problem and constraints

The API accepts guest counts under `bookings` and returns room assignments or an `error` array. The original rule definitions and allocation branches are in [`ApiController.js`](src/controllers/ApiController.js):

- Guest categories are `adult`, `children` and `infant`.
- The booking-wide capacity check counts adults and children together, with a maximum of seven; infants are excluded from that count.
- Room rules set a maximum of three for each category. Children and infants require an accompanying adult.
- The implementation distributes adults across rooms and handles minors in separate allocation branches. This is a specific exercise implementation, not a general allocation solver or a guarantee that every input ordering and boundary works.

These describe the checked-in rules, not a newly recovered or expanded interview specification.

## API examples

[`routes/index.js`](src/routes/index.js) defines `GET /api` and `POST /api/booking`. The health response is `{"message":"API Endpoint"}`.

Example request to `POST http://localhost:3000/api/booking`:

```json
{"bookings":{"adult":6}}
```

Response:

```json
{"booking":{"rooms":[{"adult":3},{"adult":3}]}}
```

Over-capacity request:

```json
{"bookings":{"adult":6,"children":2,"infant":1}}
```

Response:

```json
{"error":["Too many guests"]}
```

The original README showed that second request as a success. It exceeds the implemented non-infant capacity and has been corrected here. The original examples and historical test transcript remain in [the 2019 README at its recorded revision](https://github.com/MohdVara/nodejs-hotel-problem/blob/00b8bb09ea578232ba476a8a6b62b692ff0a15d8/README.md).

## Constraint-parser design

`initConstraint` reads `min`/`max` conditions and one level of dependent guest-category conditions from the rule objects. `checkConstraintForMultipleRooms` derives qualification information; `booking` performs allocation and formats errors. The intent was reuse across similar rules, but parsing and allocation remain in the same controller. The booking-wide capacity check is separate from the parser, and allocation contains duplicated category branches.

This separation is worth inspecting alongside its limits: coercive `parseInt` handling is not strict integer/schema validation, and the code iterates request properties while constructing rooms. No claim of complete malformed-input handling or optimal allocation is made.

## Tests and verification

[`test/test.js`](test/test.js) contains Mocha/Chai tests using mocked Express requests/responses for adult-only, mixed-guest, over-capacity, missing-data and rule-validation cases. These call controller functions; they do not establish a deployed HTTP service.

The original README recorded **25 passing tests (283 ms)** in 2019. That is historical output, **not a newly executed suite result**. No dependency installation or full application/test run was performed for this documentation update. A bounded dependency-free controller probe confirmed the two examples above using the source with only its `export function` keywords removed for a Node VM context. It also observed an initialization error for a mixed request of four adults, two children and one infant under direct current-JavaScript semantics; this probe does not reproduce the original Babel toolchain.

## Historical local setup

The repository has npm/Babel configuration but no committed lockfile or Node version pin. Inspect [`package.json`](package.json), [`.babelrc`](.babelrc) and [`nodemon.json`](nodemon.json) before attempting an isolated local reproduction.

Original commands:

```sh
npm install
npm run prod
npm test
```

These are retained as historical instructions, **not verified current setup**:

- `dev` and `prod` invoke `npm-run-all`, which is not declared in `package.json`.
- The `test` script uses a Windows-style executable path; it is not portable as written to a POSIX shell.
- `prod` cleans/builds with Babel and starts a nodemon/Babel watcher. It is not a production deployment procedure.
- The original Windows instructions suggested installing `win-node-env`; it is not a committed dependency.
- Dependency ranges are old and unlocked. Compatibility, vulnerabilities and a reproducible installation require separate maintenance work.

The server uses port 3000 by default. No current hosted deployment is verified; the old “deployment in progress” note has been retired. No runtime, dependency, script or hosting changes are included in this documentation update.

## Limitations and license

This is an interview artifact with incomplete runtime verification, coercive input handling and known allocation/tooling concerns. Do not treat it as a current security or production-readiness example. It remains available for historical inspection alongside the [current public engineering projects](https://github.com/MohdVara).

The existing [GNU GPL v3 license](LICENSE.md) is unchanged. Original implementation and commit history are preserved.
